summary: This RFC is a summary of the RFCs numbered 800 through 899. It works as an index for that range, with brief notes about each document, so readers can find which ones matter.

plainLanguage.summary: A librarian wrote a short list of what is in the hundred books on one shelf. It helps you find the right one without opening them all.

questions: history of email and domain names
subtitle: An annotated index to 100 RFCs from 1982-1984, a period of rapid internet growth.

tldr.problem: By May 1984, the RFC series had published another hundred documents. Engineers needed a current index to RFCs 800-899, many of which defined critical protocols coming into wide deployment.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 899 provides brief summaries of each RFC in the 800-899 range, organized in reverse numerical order. Each entry gives the author, date, and a concise description. The annotations highlight major protocols, policy decisions, and how newer RFCs relate to older ones.
tldr.outcome: It serves as both a status report for that period and a guide to understanding the state of Internet technology in 1984. Many protocols documented here became foundational standards.

today: RFC 899 is an Informational document and a historical record. Many of the protocols it documents remain in use; many others have been superseded. For historians, network architects studying standards evolution, and anyone tracing the development of TCP/IP, it is an invaluable reference.

sections.title: What This RFC Is
sections.content:
RFC 899 is a slightly annotated list of 100 RFCs numbered 800 through 899, published in May 1984. Like RFC 800 two years earlier, it serves as a status report and finding aid for that range of documents. The period it covers, 1982 to 1984, was one of accelerating growth: the ARPANET was consolidating with the new Internet, and protocols defined in earlier RFCs were moving from experimental to deployed.

The RFCs listed include domain name system standards, major TCP/IP refinements, Telnet options, standards for transmitting IP over local networks, and policy documents that guided the Internet's operational structure.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a list of a hundred papers from 1982-1984 about Internet technology. It tells you what each paper is about so you can find the one you need without reading them all.

sections.title: The RFCs Covered: 800-899
sections.content:
The RFCs in this range document a transitional period. Fundamental protocols like TCP and UDP were now settled (though still being refined—RFC 879 clarifies TCP's maximum segment size). The new frontier was making these protocols work reliably across diverse networks. RFC 894 specifies how to run IP over Ethernet; RFC 877 covers IP over X.25 public data networks. Both represent engineering challenges in a heterogeneous Internet.

This period also saw the domain name system emerge from proposal to specification. RFC 881 outlines the implementation plan; RFC 882 and 883 define the concepts and implementation details. RFCs 897 is a policy statement on when hosts would switch to domain names. These documents show a coordinated effort to replace ARPANET's flat namespace with a hierarchical naming scheme.
sections.plainLanguage: These papers cover a time when the Internet was growing fast and they were figuring out how to make it work across different kinds of computer networks. They also invented the domain name system so you could type 'example.com' instead of remembering numbers.

sections.title: Core Standards and Protocols
sections.content:
RFC 899 lists a cluster of foundational standards that remain in use today. Telnet options (RFCs 854-861) define the framework and many specific options. Domain names (RFC 882, 883) establish how computers find each other by name. SMTP (RFC 821) and mail-related standards (RFC 822) define how email travels. Network transmission standards specify how IP datagrams move over Ethernet (RFC 894), X.25 (RFC 877), and SATNET (RFC 890).

Many entries note obsolescence or supersession: RFC 870 obsoletes five earlier versions of the Assigned Numbers registry; RFC 821 obsoletes multiple earlier mail RFCs. This reflects the way standards evolve; old versions are documented as superseded, so implementers know to follow the latest one.
sections.plainLanguage: This list includes the rules for email, the rules for finding computers by name, the rules for connecting to a remote terminal, and the rules for sending data over different types of networks.

sections.title: Policy and Operational Documents
sections.content:
Unlike purely technical specifications, RFC 899 also includes policy statements and operational reports. RFC 890 is a policy decision on the Exterior Gateway Protocol implementation schedule. RFC 897 establishes timelines for switching to domain names. RFC 880 identifies the official protocols and their status.

Other entries are surveys: RFCs 832-846 are a series of tests to see which hosts supported TCP services like Telnet, FTP, and SMTP. These surveys offered a snapshot of how widely new protocols were deployed. When RFC 847 summarizes all the surveys, it shows that TCP adoption was growing month by month.
sections.plainLanguage: Some of these papers say 'everyone must switch to the new system by this date' or 'here's how many computers are using this technology now.' They're coordination documents, not just technical details.

sections.title: The Breadth of Internet Development
sections.content:
RFC 899 reveals how wide the Internet effort was by 1984. Technical topics range from the theoretical (RFC 889 on delay experiments and TCP timeout calculations) to the practical (RFC 810 on host tables). There are specialized protocols: RFC 887 on resource location, RFC 869 on host monitoring. There are critiques and discussions: RFC 874 offers "A Critique of X.25"; RFC 871 reflects on differences between the ARPANET Reference Model and the ISO model.

The list also includes domains beyond the core Internet—RFCs on USENET news format (RFC 850), international protocols like CCITT facsimile standards (RFC 804), and experimental work like SATNET timings. By 1984, the RFC series was documenting not just the Internet's core, but the entire ecosystem of computer networks and standards work around it.
sections.plainLanguage: These papers cover not just the main Internet, but also things connected to it: email news, fax machines, and other networks. It shows how much work was happening all around the Internet.
